title: Key highlights from Nigeria’s 2025 tax reform agenda
excerpt: A board-ready view of reform themes, compliance posture and the actions finance teams should take in the next 90 days.
keyTakeaways: Refresh CIT provisions and intercompany documentation before FIRS engagement.
Reconcile VAT and WHT monthly with schedules that support remittances.
Run a 90-day compliance health check and brief the board on cash impact.

body.heading: Why this matters now
paragraphs: Finance leaders in Nigeria are balancing day-to-day compliance with a shifting policy landscape. Tax reform discussions affect how you provision for corporate tax, document transfer pricing, and communicate with boards and investors.
This briefing summarises themes we are seeing with clients—not formal tax advice. Confirm positions with your KACERTIFIEX adviser or engagement letter before filing or restructuring.

body.heading: Corporate tax and compliance posture
paragraphs: Companies should refresh CIT computations against current rates and incentives applicable to their sector. Where group structures exist, align intercompany policies with documentation FIRS may request in a review.
SMEs should separate personal and business flows, maintain reliable books, and file on time even when cash is tight—penalties and interest compound quickly.

body.heading: Indirect tax and payroll
paragraphs: VAT and WHT processes should be reconciled monthly: output vs input VAT, WHT credits, and schedules supporting remittances. PAYE across states needs consistent employee data and timely remittance to the relevant State Internal Revenue Service.
Use the Tax Intelligence Centre calendar as a planning aid, then validate dates against your accounting year-end and state rules.

body.heading: Practical next steps
paragraphs: Run a 90-day compliance health check: filings, open assessments, and pending refunds.
Brief your board on reform scenarios and cash impact.
Book a tax planning session if you are entering a transaction, restructuring, or expanding across states.

title: Five levers Nigerian SMEs can use to stabilise cash flow
excerpt: Five disciplined levers to stabilise liquidity without sacrificing growth—built for Nigerian SME finance teams.

body.heading: 1. See cash weekly, not monthly
paragraphs: A simple 13-week cash view beats a perfect annual budget when liquidity is tight. Tie it to actual bank balances, known tax remittances, and payroll.

body.heading: 2. Shorten the order-to-cash cycle
paragraphs: Invoice on delivery, follow up on receivables by age bucket, and agree clear payment terms with key customers. Where margins allow, consider modest early-payment incentives.

body.heading: 3. Negotiate payables without damaging supply
paragraphs: Prioritise suppliers critical to revenue. Document any payment plans so tax and statutory obligations are never deferred informally.

body.heading: 4. Fix stock and margin visibility
paragraphs: Many SMEs discover cash problems late because branch or SKU-level margin is unclear. Monthly management accounts—even lightweight—surface leaks early.

body.heading: 5. Use advisory before crisis borrowing
paragraphs: Expensive short-term debt often follows absent forecasts. A focused finance diagnostic can clarify whether the issue is pricing, volume, tax timing, or working capital structure.

title: What international investors should know before entering Nigeria
excerpt: Entity design, tax registration, FX and governance—what international leadership teams should sequence before capital lands.

body.heading: Market entry structure
paragraphs: Choose entity type (e.g. limited liability company) with CAC registration, tax identification, and sector licences where required. Align ownership and control with future fundraising or JV expectations from day one.

body.heading: Tax registration and ongoing obligations
paragraphs: Register with FIRS and relevant state revenue authorities. Plan for CIT, VAT, WHT on cross-border payments, and payroll if you hire locally. Transfer pricing documentation matters when related parties trade across borders.

body.heading: Repatriation and banking
paragraphs: Understand FX policy, dividend flows, and bank KYC requirements. Treasury and intercompany agreements should match how cash will move in practice—not only on paper.

body.heading: Governance and reporting
paragraphs: Investors expect IFRS-aligned reporting, audit readiness, and clear management packs. Building these early reduces friction in diligence for later rounds or exit.

title: What belongs in a board reporting pack Nigerian directors actually use
excerpt: A practical template for monthly and quarterly packs—linking KPIs, risk, tax and cash to decisions directors must make.
keyTakeaways: Lead with cash, covenant headroom and tax obligations due in the next 90 days.
Separate operational KPIs from statutory and audit status in one dashboard view.
Document decisions and open issues so follow-through is visible meeting to meeting.

body.heading: Directors need decision-grade information
paragraphs: Boards in Nigeria often receive thick packs that bury the signal. Effective reporting starts with what must be decided this meeting—liquidity, approvals, tax exposures and material variances to plan.
Finance teams should assume directors read on mobile and in transit. One-page summaries with appendices for detail outperform narrative-only decks.

body.heading: Core sections every pack should include
paragraphs: Executive summary: cash position, forecast vs actual, top three risks and asks of the board.
Performance: revenue, margin and volume drivers by business unit where relevant.
Compliance: filing status, open tax matters, audit timeline and control exceptions.
People and governance: key hires, policy updates and related-party transactions requiring notice.

body.heading: Cadence and ownership
paragraphs: Monthly packs for operating boards; quarterly depth for audit committee themes. Assign owners for each section so the CFO is not the sole author on the night before the meeting.
KACERTIFIEX helps clients design pack templates, KPI definitions and close calendars that boards can rely on.

title: Transfer pricing in Nigeria: documentation directors should not defer
excerpt: When related-party charges trigger FIRS scrutiny—and how to build defensible policies before a review starts.
keyTakeaways: Map all related-party flows: goods, services, royalties, management fees and loans.
Align transfer pricing policy to how the business actually operates, not only to templates.
Prepare local file support before FIRS requests it—not after an assessment letter arrives.

body.heading: Why transfer pricing is on the agenda
paragraphs: Groups with cross-border or related-party transactions in Nigeria face increasing expectation that charges are arm's length and documented. Manufacturing, energy, financial services and tech platforms are common focus areas.
Directors should treat transfer pricing as a governance topic, not only a tax department task.

body.heading: Building a defensible policy
paragraphs: Start with a transaction map: who sells what to whom, how prices are set, and which entities retain risk and reward.
Select methods appropriate to each transaction type and maintain contemporaneous support—contracts, benchmarking rationale and board approvals where material.

body.heading: When to involve advisers
paragraphs: Before restructuring, entering new markets or after receiving FIRS correspondence, a focused diagnostic prevents expensive rework.
Our tax practice supports policy design, documentation and structured engagement with authorities.
